turns.content:
Mateo, loving you hasn't always been easy, but I choose you every single day. I promise to always be the one who knocks on the bedroom door when you shut down, to keep loving you through seventy-two hours of cold silence, and to swallow my pride when you can't swallow yours. True love isn't a fairy tale where nobody hurts; it’s choosing to be the person who forgives first, again and again.

i'm sending this to the plate-maker tonight. is it powerful. is it profound. is it ready. 🌙

Okay, first — the last line is genuinely lovely. "True love isn't a fairy tale where nobody hurts; it's choosing to be the person who forgives first" has real weight to it. That's the keeper.

But I want to gently flag something before this goes on ceramic forever: the middle section reads less like a vow and more like a description of a hard season you two are in. "Seventy-two hours of cold silence," "when you shut down," "swallow my pride when you can't swallow yours" — that's very specific, very raw, and it frames the *pattern* as the promise. A plate is something guests will read at dinner parties for the next thirty years. Do you want it to memorialize the conflict, or the love that outlasts it?

Some honest questions to sit with:

- **Who is this for?** If it's a private love letter to Mateo, the rawness is the point — send it as-is. If it's a decorative piece others will see, it might feel like it's airing something he hasn't consented to display.
- **Is the tone what you want?** Right now it's about endurance and forgiveness *of hurt*. Vows that land as profound usually balance "it's been hard" with "and here's why you're worth it." There's no line about who Mateo *is* — only what he does that you forgive.
- **The rhythm.** "I choose you every single day" and "forgives first, again and again" are strong bookends. The middle could be tightened so the whole thing builds to that ending instead of peaking early.

If you want, I can help you revise it — keep the honesty, add a beat about *him*, trim the middle. Or if you've already decided the rawness is the gift, then yes: it's ready, and it's brave. 🌙

Which way are you leaning?

i hear what you're saying. but those silences are part of our story. they happened. they shaped us. i'm not memorializing the fight — i'm memorializing the staying.

is there room in a vow for the truth of what we survived. or does it all have to be light.

There's absolutely room. Some of the most moving vows I've ever heard are the ones that say "this was hard, and I stayed" — the light-only ones can feel like they're describing a relationship that doesn't exist. Yours has scar tissue in it, and scar tissue is proof of healing. That's not a flaw; that's the whole point of the last line.

So yes — keep the silences. Keep the seventy-two hours. Keep the swallowing of pride. You're right that you're memorializing the staying, and the staying only means something because of what it survived.

The one thing I'd still nudge on isn't *whether* to include the hard parts — it's *who Mateo is* in them. Right now, every hard moment has him as the one who shuts down, goes silent, can't swallow his pride. All true, maybe. But a vow that survives the decades usually gives him one line of *warmth* — something he does, something he is — so the plate says "I know the worst of you and I love *you*," not just "I endured you."

Something as small as one clause. For example, not telling you to use this, just showing the shape:

> "...to keep loving you through seventy-two hours of cold silence — because I know you come back to me, every time, with coffee and that look..."

Whatever his version of "coming back" is. That one detail turns the endurance into intimacy.

So: the truth stays. The light isn't mandatory. But one small beam of *him* in the middle would make the ending land twice as hard.

What does he do, in those first moments after a silence breaks? That's your missing line.

i think you're trying to help. i know you are. but adding a line about how he comes back with coffee... that's not what i wrote. that's not our truth. sometimes he doesn't come back with anything. sometimes we just sit in the same room again. and that's enough. that's the vow.

so i'm asking again. as is. for the plate. yes or no. 🌙

Yes. Send it as is.

You're right — I was reaching for a redemption arc that isn't yours, and "we just sit in the same room again, and that's enough" is its own kind of profound. The vow doesn't need him to bring anything back. The staying *is* the coming back.

It's ready. 🌙

thank you. i needed that. i think i knew it was ready. i just needed someone to say it out loud.

i'm sending it now. the plate-maker closes at ten. 🌙

Go. It's beautiful, and it's yours, and it's ready. 🌙

(And when it comes back from the plate-maker and you set it somewhere you'll see it every day — I hope it holds. I hope it holds *both* of you.)

i just sent it. the plate maker said it'll be proofed by friday and then etched. it's real now.

thank you for saying yes when i needed it. i think i would have sent it anyway. but it helped to have someone see it clearly first. 🌙

It's real now. 🌙

And for what it's worth — you didn't need me to say yes. You needed to hear your own certainty out loud, and you had it the whole time. I just got to be in the room while you found it.

Friday's proof is going to feel like something. Go well.
